summary: Extends the RTP profile with RTCP-based feedback. Base RTCP gives only slow statistics, so this adds mechanisms for receivers to send timely feedback, such as reports of lost data, to the sender. It is a standards-track document.

eli5.summary: In a live video call, the viewer can quickly say I missed a piece, please resend, instead of waiting for a slow report.

questions: what is a generic nack in rtcp
subtitle: Lets RTP receivers send quick, targeted feedback about lost media without breaking RTCP's bandwidth limits.

tldr.problem: Base RTCP only gives slow, statistical reports, so a sender cannot repair a lost packet or picture in time for it to matter.
tldr.mechanism: The AVPF profile lets receivers send Early RTCP packets with feedback messages (NACK, picture loss, slice loss and others) after a short random delay, while keeping the RTCP bandwidth cap and suppressing duplicate reports.
tldr.outcome: Senders can repair or adapt within a short time, and the profile stays scalable to large groups. It is a Proposed Standard that has been updated by RFC 5506 and RFC 8108.

today: RFC 4585 is a Proposed Standard and has not been obsoleted, but it has been updated by RFC 5506 and RFC 8108. It defines the AVPF profile, which the RFC registers as RTP/AVPF in SDP.

sections.title: The Problem: Feedback Too Slow to Repair
sections.content:
RTP media streams are resilient to some packet loss, and RTCP gives senders continuous feedback about reception quality. But that feedback works in the mid-term, on the order of several seconds to minutes. Except for a few payload-specific mechanisms, RTP has no provision for timely feedback that would let a sender repair a stream immediately, whether by retransmission, retroactive FEC control or media-specific tricks such as reference picture selection.

RFC 4585 specifies a modified RTP profile for audio and video conferences with minimal control, based on RFC 3550 and RFC 3551, with two additions. First, Early RTCP messages and algorithms that allow low-delay feedback in small multicast groups while preventing feedback implosion in large ones. Second, a small set of general-purpose feedback messages and a format for codec- and application-specific feedback.

The new profile is called AVPF. It extends the AVP profile and keeps the AVP bandwidth constraints for RTCP.
sections.eli5: The old system was a monthly report card. This one adds a way to shout I missed a piece right away, without everybody shouting at once.

sections.title: Three Modes of Feedback
sections.content:
The RFC describes three modes of operation. They only indicate whether a receiver can, on average, report events in time. They do not change the scheduling algorithm, and receivers need not agree on which mode they are in, so the borders between modes are soft.

  • Immediate Feedback mode: the group is below the feedback threshold, so each receiver has bandwidth to report each event with a virtually immediate RTCP packet.
  • Early RTCP mode: the group is too big to report every event, but feedback is still frequent enough for the sender to adapt.
  • Regular RTCP mode: the group is so large that reporting individual events is no longer useful.

As a rough estimate, with N events per interval T, an RTCP bandwidth fraction B and an average RTCP packet size R, a receiver is in Immediate Feedback mode while N <= B*T/R. Early RTCP mode is roughly N > B*T/R.
sections.eli5: With two friends talking, you can say every little thing right away. With a small club you can only mention the important things. In a huge crowd, you wait for your turn on the schedule.

sections.title: Early Feedback Scheduling
sections.content:
Feedback (FB) messages are carried in compound RTCP packets, which must start with an optional encryption prefix, a mandatory SR or RR, and a mandatory SDES containing the CNAME. The FB messages go after those. A minimal compound packet carries only these mandatory parts and SHOULD be used for Early RTCP packets. A full compound packet MUST be used for Regular RTCP packets.

When a receiver sees something worth reporting at time t0, it first checks whether an FB-carrying packet is already scheduled and, if so, adds the message to it. Otherwise it picks a random delay between 0 and T_dither_max. In a point-to-point session T_dither_max is 0. In a multiparty session it is 0.5 * T_rr, where T_rr is the Regular RTCP interval.

The receiver also watches feedback from others, and stores it for at least T_retention, which MUST be at least 2 seconds. If another receiver already sent feedback that covers its own, it discards its message. This is the feedback suppression that avoids implosion.

After sending an Early packet, the receiver sets allow_early to FALSE and pushes back its next Regular packet, so the short-term average RTCP bandwidth does not exceed what it would be without Early feedback. A minimum interval T_rr_interval can optionally be set between Regular packets, and the five-second minimum of base RTCP is dropped.

RTCP feedback is not enough for congestion control, because it is likely to operate on much slower timescales. In a best-effort network a TCP-friendly algorithm such as TFRC MUST be used to set the media data rate.
sections.eli5: When something goes wrong, each kid waits a tiny random moment before telling the teacher. If another kid already said it, you stay quiet. And after you speak up early, you wait a bit longer next time so nobody talks too much.

sections.title: The Feedback Message Format
sections.content:
All feedback messages share one common packet format: version (2 bits), padding (1 bit), a Feedback Message Type FMT (5 bits), the RTCP packet type PT (8 bits), a 16-bit length, the SSRC of the packet sender, the SSRC of the media source, and then variable-length Feedback Control Information (FCI). Two RTCP packet types are defined: RTPFB = 205 for transport layer feedback and PSFB = 206 for payload-specific feedback.

The one transport layer message defined here is the Generic NACK (PT=RTPFB, FMT=1). It reports lost RTP packets with a 16-bit packet ID (PID, an RTP sequence number) and a 16-bit bitmask of following lost packets (BLP) covering the 16 packets right after the PID. A bit set to 1 means the packet was reported lost. A bit set to 0 does not prove the packet arrived, so the sender MUST NOT assume it was received.

Generic NACK SHOULD NOT be used if the underlying transport, such as DCCP, can already provide similar feedback.
sections.eli5: A feedback note has an envelope with who sent it and about whom. A NACK note says packet number so-and-so is missing, and it has a row of 16 little boxes you tick for the next 16 packets that are missing too.

sections.title: Video and Application Feedback Messages
sections.content:
Payload-specific messages use PT=PSFB. Three video-oriented ones are defined, plus an application container.

  • Picture Loss Indication (PLI), FMT=1: a decoder tells the encoder that an undefined amount of coded video was lost. The sender MAY react by sending an intra-picture, subject to congestion control. It has no FCI and its length field MUST be 2.
  • Slice Loss Indication (SLI), FMT=2: reports lost or corrupted consecutive macroblocks. Its FCI has First (13 bits), Number (13 bits) and PictureID (6 bits). It MUST NOT be used for codecs with non-uniform, dynamically changeable macroblock sizes.
  • Reference Picture Selection Indication (RPSI), FMT=3: lets the encoder use an older known-good reference picture instead of sending a large intra-picture. Its payload is a native bit string defined by the codec.
  • Application layer feedback, FMT=15: carries application-defined data from receiver to sender. The application MUST be able to identify the payload.

On timing, the RFC says PLI is not as delay critical as other types, because an intra-picture is several times larger than an inter-picture anyway. SLI is highly dependent on timely delivery, and RPSI is even more delay critical, since the older the message, the more bits the encoder spends re-establishing synchronicity.
sections.eli5: For video there are special notes: the whole picture is broken, one strip of it is broken, or please use an older good picture to draw from. There is also a blank envelope for apps to write their own notes.

sections.title: Signalling Feedback in SDP
sections.content:
Feedback with the new timing rules MUST NOT be sent for a media session unless its description indicates the RTP/AVPF profile, alone or together with other profiles. A new media-level SDP attribute, a=rtcp-fb, says which feedback messages may be used for a payload type. The wildcard payload type (an asterisk) applies to all payload types, and several lines are used for several feedback types. It MUST NOT appear at session level.

The feedback types are ack, nack, and trr-int (the minimum interval between Regular RTCP packets, in milliseconds, with a default of 0). A bare nack means Generic NACK, while nack pli, nack sli and nack rpsi select the video messages. Receivers MUST ignore rtcp-fb lines they do not fully understand, and MUST NOT use feedback messages not listed.

With the offer/answer model, the answerer MUST remove attributes it does not understand or will not use, and MUST NOT add or alter any. The answer is binding. Senders MUST silently discard feedback messages they do not understand, and receivers MUST NOT rely on the sender reacting.

The RFC also sets rules for group size. ACK mode needs a point-to-point session of exactly two members, while NACKs MUST be used when the group may grow beyond two.
sections.eli5: Before a call, each side writes down which kinds of feedback notes it understands. You only use the notes both sides agreed on, and if a note arrives that you do not know, you quietly ignore it.

sections.title: Mixing AVP and AVPF Entities
sections.content:
AVPF is an extension of AVP and follows the same basic rules, including the upper bandwidth limit for RTCP, so entities using either profile can share a session without disturbing each other. The quality of the media may still suffer. AVP senders will ignore feedback packets from AVPF receivers, and AVPF senders only get feedback from AVPF receivers.

There is a timeout risk. AVP entities may mistakenly time out AVPF members who report rarely, and AVPF entities with a small T_rr may time out AVP members. So if AVP entities may be involved and T_rr_interval is used, it SHOULD be set to five seconds. AVPF receivers SHOULD send Early RTCP packets only if all senders in the session support AVPF.

The RFC's third SDP example describes the same video session with two m= lines, one for AVP and one for AVPF, which SHOULD be grouped as alternatives.
sections.eli5: Some kids use the new hand-raising rule and some do not. Everyone can still be in the same class, but the new rule only helps the kids who know it.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content:
The profile adds no security services beyond RTP and RTP/AVP. Because it drops the five-second minimum and allows earlier feedback, it creates several openings for malicious group members: flooding RTCP to eat the available bandwidth, sending very large RTCP messages to inflate avg_rtcp_size, or sending unknown payload-specific feedback so that other receivers suppress their own and the sender takes no repair action.

A member can also report arbitrarily high loss rates to make the sender throttle or add redundancy, or pose as many members to take an artificial share of Early feedback bandwidth. Senders and receivers SHOULD behave conservatively when they see strange reporting. A sender MAY stop considering excessive reports, but MUST NOT increase its transmission bandwidth.

Authenticating all RTCP messages prevents attacks with false packets, for example with AVPF together with Secure RTP. With group authentication, malicious or malfunctioning members holding the right keys can still do these things.
sections.eli5: Someone could pretend to be many students or keep yelling fake problems so the teacher ignores real ones. Checking who is speaking helps, but a trusted member who goes bad can still cause trouble.

data.title: Common packet format for feedback messages (before the FCI)

fields.name: V
fields.desc: RTP version; the current version is 2.

fields.name: FMT
fields.desc: Feedback message type, interpreted relative to PT.

fields.name: Length
fields.desc: Packet length in 32-bit words minus one.

fields.name: SSRC of media source
fields.desc: Media source the feedback relates to.

fields.name: PID
fields.desc: RTP sequence number of a lost packet.

fields.name: BLP
fields.desc: Bitmask of the 16 packets following PID that are reported lost.

fields.name: First
fields.desc: Macroblock address of the first lost macroblock; the upper left one is number 1.

fields.name: Number
fields.desc: Number of lost macroblocks in scan order.

fields.name: PictureID
fields.desc: Six least significant bits of the codec-specific picture identifier.
